questions.question: How do you test asynchronous code and CompletableFuture in Java?
questions.title: Testing Async / CompletableFuture Code
questions.direct_answer: For CompletableFuture, call .get() or .join() in the test to block until the result is available, then assert on it. For @Async Spring methods, either use CountDownLatch/CompletableFuture to wait, or test the underlying method directly without the async wrapper in unit tests. For reactive code (Mono/Flux), use StepVerifier. Avoid Thread.sleep() — it makes tests slow and flaky.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the challenges of non-deterministic async execution in tests and how to avoid Thread.sleep()
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Thread.sleep() to wait for async results — it makes tests slow and still flaky; use blocking get() or Awaitility instead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Awaitility for testing @Async side effects (like database writes triggered asynchronously) without sleep, and how to test exception propagation in CompletableFuture

sections.title: Thread.sleep() in Async Tests Is a Bug, Not a Strategy
sections.content:
Testing asynchronous code requires synchronization between the test thread and the async execution. The naive approach — `Thread.sleep(2000)` — is both slow (always waits the full duration) and flaky (fails when execution takes longer than expected on a loaded CI server).

`CompletableFuture` testing is simpler than it appears because the future itself provides the synchronization point. Call `.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` or `.join()` with a timeout — the test blocks until the result is available or times out.

The harder case is testing `@Async` methods in Spring, where the method returns before the async work completes. Here you need an explicit synchronization mechanism: `CountDownLatch`, `Awaitility`, or a `CompletableFuture` that the async code completes. The test waits on this mechanism with a timeout, proceeding as soon as the async work finishes.

The key principle: **every async test needs an explicit synchronization point.** For `CompletableFuture`, the future itself is the synchronization. For `@Async void` methods, you create one — typically by observing a side effect (database write, event, flag). The test waits on this synchronization point with a timeout, never on a fixed sleep duration. Awaitility provides this pattern out of the box with `await().atMost().untilAsserted()`, polling the assertion until it passes or the timeout expires.

sections.title: Testing CompletableFuture — The Future IS the Synchronization
Testing @Async Methods — When the Method Returns void
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
For `CompletableFuture`, the future itself is your synchronization point — call `.get(5, SECONDS)` and assert on the result. No `Thread.sleep()` needed. For failures, `future.get()` wraps the exception in `ExecutionException`, so assert on the cause.

The harder case is `@Async void` methods. There's no future to wait on, so you need to observe a side effect. **Awaitility** is the standard tool: `await().atMost(10, SECONDS).untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(...))`. It polls the assertion until it passes or times out — adapting to actual execution speed instead of sleeping for an arbitrary duration.

`Thread.sleep()` is always wrong in tests. It's too slow (always waits the full duration) and too flaky (fails when CI is loaded). Every async test should use either the future's `.get()` or Awaitility.

Remember: `@Async` requires Spring's proxy, so these tests need `@SpringBootTest` with `@EnableAsync`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Thread.sleep()` is always wrong in async tests** — too slow (always waits full duration) and too flaky (fails on loaded CI); use `future.get(timeout)` or Awaitility instead.
- **`CompletableFuture.get()` IS the synchronization point** — blocks until result is available; JUnit 5's `assertTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5), () -> future.get())` provides clear failure messages.
- **`await().atMost().untilAsserted()` polls until the assertion passes** — adapts to actual execution speed; fast locally, tolerant of CI slowness; standard for testing `@Async void` methods.
- **`@Async` methods need `@SpringBootTest` + `@EnableAsync`** — the async proxy is created by Spring's post-processor; without a Spring context, the method runs synchronously and the test passes for the wrong reason.
- **`future.get()` wraps exceptions in `ExecutionException`** — use `.hasCauseInstanceOf()` to assert on the actual exception; direct `assertThrows(UserNotFoundException.class)` won't match.

questions.question: Code Coverage with JaCoCo — What to Measure and What to Ignore
questions.title: Code Coverage with JaCoCo — What to Measure and What to Ignore
questions.direct_answer: JaCoCo measures how much code is executed during tests. Line coverage counts executed lines. Branch coverage counts executed decision paths. Coverage measures test execution, not test quality.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands what code coverage measures, its limitations, and what coverage targets are meaningful.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Chasing 100% coverage by testing getters, setters, and trivial code — this adds test maintenance cost without catching bugs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain branch coverage vs line coverage, why coverage targets should differ by code type (80%+ for business logic, lower for configuration), and how JaCoCo exclusions prevent misleading metrics.

sections.title: 100% Coverage Doesn't Mean Zero Bugs — It Means Every Line Was Executed, Not Verified
sections.content:
Code coverage measures what percentage of your code runs during tests. **Line coverage** counts lines executed. **Branch coverage** counts decision paths taken — both the `if` and `else` branches. JaCoCo is the standard coverage tool for Java projects, integrated into Maven/Gradle and CI pipelines.

The misconception: high coverage = good tests. A test that calls every method but asserts nothing has 100% coverage and catches zero bugs. Coverage measures **execution, not verification.** A line is "covered" if it ran during any test, regardless of whether the test checked the output.

The practical target: **80% line coverage for business logic, lower for configuration and boilerplate.** Chasing 100% means testing getters, setters, generated code, and exception paths that add maintenance cost without catching bugs. The last 20% of coverage typically requires 80% of the testing effort — and that effort is better spent on edge cases in critical code than on covering trivial code.

Branch coverage is more valuable than line coverage. A method with an `if/else` can have 100% line coverage (both branches run) but if you only test the `true` branch, you miss bugs in the `false` path. JaCoCo tracks both and reports them separately.

sections.title: Configuring JaCoCo With Meaningful Exclusions
sections.content:
JaCoCo integrates with Maven via the `jacoco-maven-plugin`. The key configuration is **exclusions** — removing code that shouldn't affect your coverage metric.

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
    <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <excludes>
            <exclude>**/config/**</exclude>
            <exclude>**/dto/**</exclude>
            <exclude>**/*Application.class</exclude>
            <exclude>**/generated/**</exclude>
        </excludes>
    </configuration>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>
        </execution>
        <execution>
            <id>report</id>
            <phase>verify</phase>
            <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

Exclude configuration classes (pure Spring wiring), DTOs (data carriers with no logic), the main application class, and generated code (MapStruct, Lombok). Without exclusions, these inflate your coverage denominator — making it harder to reach meaningful coverage targets for actual business logic.

For enforcement, add a `check` goal with `BUNDLE` rules: `LINE` minimum 0.80, `BRANCH` minimum 0.70. JaCoCo fails the build if coverage drops below the threshold. Set thresholds per package if different areas have different complexity levels.

sections.title: What to Measure and What to Ignore — The Coverage Strategy
sections.content:
**High coverage targets (80%+):** business logic services, domain models, validators, calculators. This is where bugs live and where tests provide the most value. Branch coverage matters here — every `if/else` decision path should be tested.

**Moderate coverage (60-80%):** controllers, mappers, integration code. These are mostly wiring — the framework does most of the work. Test the important paths (validation, error handling) but don't force coverage on trivial mappings.

**Low or excluded:** configuration classes, DTOs, generated code, the main class. Testing `@Bean` definitions and data carriers adds maintenance cost without catching bugs.

The coverage report should be a conversation tool, not a gate. A team that discusses uncovered branches in code review catches more bugs than a team that mandates 90% coverage and writes `@Test void testGetters()` to hit the number.

One metric worth tracking: **coverage of changed code.** CI tools like SonarQube measure "coverage on new code" separately. Requiring 80% coverage on new code is more effective than requiring 80% overall — it ensures new features are tested without forcing retroactive testing of legacy code.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JaCoCo measures test execution, not test quality. A test that calls every method but asserts nothing has 100% coverage and catches zero bugs. Coverage tells you what code ran during tests — not whether the tests actually verified anything.

Branch coverage is more valuable than line coverage. A method with `if/else` can show 100% line coverage while only testing the `true` branch. JaCoCo reports both separately.

My target: 80%+ for business logic, 60-80% for controllers and mappers, and exclude configuration classes and DTOs entirely. Chasing 100% means testing getters and generated code — maintenance cost with zero bug-catching value.

The most useful metric is **coverage on new code** — requiring 80% on changed files ensures new features are tested without forcing retroactive coverage of legacy code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Coverage measures execution, not verification** — a line is "covered" if it ran during any test, regardless of assertions; 100% coverage with no assertions catches nothing.
- **Branch coverage > line coverage** — `if/else` can show 100% line coverage while testing only one path; branch coverage ensures both decision paths are exercised.
- **Exclude config, DTOs, generated code from coverage** — these inflate the denominator without representing testable logic; without exclusions, reaching 80% forces testing getters and setters.
- **80%+ for business logic, lower for wiring code** — different code types warrant different targets; controllers and mappers are mostly framework code with less bug surface.
- **"Coverage on new code" is the most actionable metric** — requiring 80% on changed files ensures new features are tested; avoids the retroactive testing problem with legacy code.
